
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
source("common.R")
```

# Visual Shapes {#sec-visual-shapes}

All of the data visualisations that we have considered so far
have encoded a **single data value** from one or more variables
to a **single data symbol** (@fig-multivariate-symbol-a).
For example, a bar plot like @fig-bar encodes the number of offenders
for one ethnic group to one
bar.  A scatter plot like @fig-scatter encodes the number of clean breaks
and the number of tries for one team to one data point.

In this chapter, we consider data visualisations that encode **multiple
data values** from one or more variables to a **single data symbol**
(@fig-multivariate-symbol-b).
In this chapter, we begin to consider more complex data symbols
that produce **visual shapes**.[^point-shape]

[^point-shape]:
    In this chapter, we focus on data symbols that represent multiple
    sets of data values, like lines.
    It could be argued that there are data symbols that are visual shapes
    that arise from encoding a single, qualitative data value 
    to a data symbol, for example,
    different data points---circles versus triangles versus squares---in 
    a scatter plot.
    However, in this book, that case is referred to as a encoding
    from qualitative data value to the *pattern*---a basic visual
    feature---of a data symbol (@sec-visual-features).

::: {#fig-multivariate-symbol}

::: {.content-visible when-format=pdf layout-ncol=2}
::: {#fig-multivariate-symbol-a}
\includegraphics[scale=0.7]{Mappings/mapping-1-2-1-2.png}
:::
::: {#fig-multivariate-symbol-b}
\includegraphics[scale=0.7]{Mappings/mapping-2-2-1-2.png}
:::
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format=html layout-ncol=2}
![Each row of data values encodes to one data symbol.](Mappings/mapping-1-2-1-2.png){#fig-multivariate-symbol-a}

![Multiple rows of data values encode to one data symbol.](Mappings/mapping-2-2-1-2.png){#fig-multivariate-symbol-b}
:::

\(a) A simple data symbol, like a bar in a bar plot or a data point in a
scatter plot involves encoding **one** row of data values
to the visual features of 
**one** data symbol;  a single pair of data values
produces a single data symbol (this is a reproduction of the diagram in 
@fig-two-visual-features).
\(b) A more complex data symbol is produced if we encode
**multiple** rows of data values to the 
visual features of **one** data symbol.
Multiple data values from `x` and `y` are encoded to the visual
features, `a` and `b`, of a single data symbol.
Multiple pairs of values produce a single data symbol.
:::

## Line plots {#sec-line-plots}

@fig-line shows a line plot of the number of offenders per year 
in different ethnic 
groups from 2011 to 2021 (@tbl-crime-group-year).
This data visualisation is very effective for perceiving changes
over time in the number of offenders within each group as well as
comparing the changes over time between groups.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-line
#| fig-cap: A line plot of the number of offenders per year in different ethnic groups from 2011 to 2021.
gg <- ggplot(crimeGroup) +
    geom_line(aes(year, count, colour=group)) +
    scale_x_continuous(name=NULL, breaks=seq(2012, 2020, 2)) +    
    scale_y_continuous(expand=expansion(c(0, .05))) +
    scale_colour_npg(name="ethnic group") +
    theme(aspect.ratio=1)
pushViewport(viewport(width=.8, height=.8))
print(gg, newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
```

There are some familiar encodings in this data visualisation: year
is encoded to horizontal **position**, the number of offenders
is encoded to vertical **position**, and the ethnic group is encoded
to **colour**.
However, the **data symbols** in this data visualisation, the coloured lines,
are different
from any previous examples that we have seen.
Although there are 44 rows of data, there are only 4 data symbols.
Multiple rows of data are used to create each data symbol.
Each coloured line in @fig-line represents 11 pairs of year and count values.

This contrasts with visualisations like bar plots that use simpler data symbols.
For example, the bar plot of the same data in @fig-side-bar-year has
44 data symbols (44 bars).

@fig-line is effective at conveying changes over time because the
coloured lines create **visual shapes** (@fig-data-vis-shape)
and those visual shapes convey information about collections of data
values.
For example, we can perceive slopes and curves and peaks and valleys
in each of the coloured lines.[^Visual_Pattern_Rec]

[^Visual_Pattern_Rec]:
    @Few2006 [p. 10] discusses this difference in a comparison between 
    a density plot (mostly see a shape) and a
    histogram (mostly see bar heights).

::: {#fig-data-vis-shape}
::: {.content-visible when-format=pdf layout-ncol=2}
\includegraphics[scale=0.5]{Diagrams/data-vis-shape.png}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format=html layout-ncol=2}
![](Diagrams/data-vis-shape.png)
:::

If we encode multiple data values to multiple visual features of
a single data symbol, like in a line plot, 
we create a smaller number of more complex data symbols, **visual shapes**,
that contain a larger amount of information.
:::

By comparison, in @fig-no-line, 
which encodes each data value to its own data symbol,
it is much harder to decode the slopes, curves, peaks, and valleys.
Despite the colours of the data symbols, it is even harder
to group the different sets of data symbols together;
the connecting lines between the data values in @fig-line are a very strong
encoding that the data values belong to the same ethnic group 
(@sec-visual-model-groups).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-no-line
#| fig-cap: A scatter plot of the number of offenders per year in different ethnic groups from 2011 to 2021.
gg <- ggplot(crimeGroup) +
    geom_point(aes(year, count, colour=group)) +
    scale_x_continuous(name=NULL, breaks=seq(2012, 2020, 2)) +    
    scale_colour_npg(name="ethnic group") +
    theme(aspect.ratio=1)
pushViewport(viewport(width=.8, height=.8))
print(gg, newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
```

In terms of the simple visual processing model from @sec-visual-processing,
these more complicated shapes can convey higher-level information,
at the expense of a little more visual processing, and with a limit on how many
shapes we can process simultaneously
(@fig-visual-model).
In terms of [Chapter 8](summaries.html), 
the more complex data symbols create visual shapes that allow us to decode
**data summaries** (@fig-data-vis-shape-decode).
For example, in @fig-line we are able to decode
data summaries such as the overall trends in the number
of offenders, periods of more rapid change versus periods of slower
change, and local maxima and minima.[^lines-as-shapes]

[^lines-as-shapes]:
    "not only is a line a single perceptual unit, and
    hence there will be less to hold in short-term memory, but we are good at
    detecting slope differences---which convey the relevant information"
    [@kosslyn1989understanding, p. 211] 

::: {#fig-data-vis-shape-decode}
::: {.content-visible when-format=pdf layout-ncol=2}
\includegraphics[scale=0.5]{Diagrams/data-vis-shape-decode.png}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format=html layout-ncol=2}
![](Diagrams/data-vis-shape-decode.png)
:::

If we encode data values to a **visual shape**
that contains a large amount of information,
then we may be able to decode higher-level **data summaries**.
:::

This ability to decode data summaries, such as peaks and slopes,
when we use lines as data symbols is even more apparent if we
compare @fig-line with @fig-side-bar-year.  When we have bars as
data symbols, these data summaries are much less apparent.

In terms of @sec-congruence, 
the use of lines for data symbols is also **congruent** with
trends in the data;  we naturally associate slopes with increases
and decreases in data values.[^line-trends]
For example, it is very natural to decode a downward trend from the
lines in a line plot like
@fig-crime.  While it is also possible to decode trends from the
coloured rectangles in a heatmap like @fig-crime-heatmap, the 
decoding is less immediately obvious.

[^line-trends]:
    According to @Zacks1999
    people use *trend words* (increasing/decreasing) versus *discrete words*
    (higher/lower than) *and* are faster to judge absolute values from bars
    but angle from line graphs.

> One reason why line plots are effective is because they encode multiple
  data values into a complex data symbol that creates a visual shape,
  from which we are able to decode data summaries.

On the other hand, the more complex data symbols in a line plot,
where each data symbol
contains multiple data values, are less effective at encoding
the *individual* raw data values. 
The coloured lines in @fig-line are not simple shapes
from which it is easy to decode basic **visual features**.
This means that, although we may be able to decode data summaries,
it is not as easy to decode the raw data values
(@fig-data-vis-shape-decode).
For example, compare the ease with which we can
determine the number of European/Other
offenders in 2013 from @fig-line versus @fig-side-bar-year.
@fig-side-bar-year has simple data symbols that encode a single
data value as a basic visual feature of a single data symbol---the
length of a bar---so we can easily decode the individual raw data values
from the bars.

This deficiency is significant because the main encodings in a line plot
are from **quantitative** data values to (horizontal and vertical) **position**.
We know from @sec-encoding-visual-features that these should be very
effective encodings that allow us to accurately decode the raw data values.
However, in a line plot, we are not encoding a single data value to a
basic visual feature of a single, simple shape.  Instead, a single data value 
is being encoded, along with many other values,
to a basic visual feature of a complicated shape.  In effect, the
individual data values lose their individual identity.[^non-injective]

[^non-injective]:
    @Ziemkiewicz2009 refer to this as a *non-injective* encoding
    and point out that it makes it impossible for there to be a
    decoding, because multiple data values encode to the same
    data symbol.  This is in contrast to a *bijective* encoding,
    which is one-to-one between data values and data symbols
    (@sec-bar).

    This problem also relates to the issue of drawing data symbols 
    on top of each other (@sec-pos-scarce).
    If two data symbols completely overlap, for example if two
    data points on a scatterplot overlap, then it is impossible to
    decode both individual data values.

    Figure 4.5 of 
    @Bartonicek_thesis2023 has an interesting, if pathological, demonstration
    of this problem using a simple bar plot.
    The bar plot has a single bar that represents the sum of counts for two
    categories.
    In this demonstration 
    there is also a bar just for one of the counts, so that, with
    unnecessary mental effort, it is possible to recover the "hidden"
    data value, but we can imagine 
    an even more pathological demonstration which would 
    encode two data values to a single bar, without encoding one of the data
    values to its own bar.  In that case it would be
    completely impossible to decode the two data values from the 
    single bar.

> One reason why a line plot is *less* effective for decoding
  raw data values is because each raw data value is not encoded to its
  own data symbol.

The creation of visual shapes from multiple data values
bears some similarity to the creation of emergent features by
combining visual features (@sec-integral).  In both cases,
we have *explicit* encodings from data values to basic visual features,
but we also produce an *implicit* additional visual effect.
The difference here is that, with visual shapes, we are collapsing
multiple data values into a data symbol, so we run a higher risk
of losing the ability to perceive individual data values.[^lines-configural]

[^lines-configural]:
    @Peebles2008 describes a line plot as *configural*---rather than either
    *separable* (@sec-separable) or *integral* (@sec-integral)---which 
    means that it is possible to decode individual data values and
    data summaries, but that configural displays
    lead to poorer decoding of individual data values.
    This also 
    links to the *display proximity principal* [@proximity-compatibility].

There is also a similarity between visual shapes and visual summaries 
(@sec-visual-summaries).  In both cases, we gain the ability to decode
data summaries from collections of data values.
The difference is that, with visual summaries, we are summarising
many simple data symbols that each represent individual data values, 
whereas with a visual shape we decode the
data summary from a single data symbol that obscures the individual data values.
In the case of a visual summary, the individual data values can still be 
decoded, but with a visual shape that is more difficult.

## Case study:  Scatter plots with lines

@fig-line-points shows a data visualisation of the number of offenders
per year in different ethnic groups (@tbl-crime-group-year).
This is very similar to @fig-line, but we have added a data point
at every horizontal and vertical **position** as well as the lines
between positions.

Like @fig-line, we can decode overall trends from the line data symbols,
but we can also decode individual data values more easily because
now every individual data value is also encoded to its own data symbol.
By employing both simple data symbols that encode individual data values
and complex data symbols that encode multiple data values as visual
shapes, we get the best of both worlds.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-line-points
#| fig-cap: A plot of the number of offenders per year in different ethnic groups from 2011 to 2021 with both lines and points.
gg <- ggplot(crimeGroup) +
    geom_line(aes(year, count, colour=group)) +
    geom_point(aes(year, count, colour=group), 
               pch=21, fill=figbg, stroke=1) +
    scale_x_continuous(name=NULL, breaks=seq(2012, 2020, 2)) +    
    scale_colour_npg(name="ethnic group") +
    theme(aspect.ratio=1)
pushViewport(viewport(width=.8, height=.8))
print(gg, newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
```

## Case study: Density plots {#sec-density}

@fig-density shows a density plot of the number of points scored by Tier One
nations at the Rugby World Cups (@tbl-rwc-all).
As with a histogram (@fig-hist), this data visualisation is effective
for conveying the distribution of data values.
For example, we can decode that there is evidence of 
a single mode and right skew.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-density
#| fig-cap: A density plot of the points scored per game by Tier One nations at Rugby World Cups.
gg <- ggplot(rwcAll) +
    geom_density(aes(scored), colour="black", linewidth=1) +
    scale_x_continuous(name="points scored") +
    theme(axis.title.y=element_blank(),
          axis.text.y=element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.y=element_blank())
pushViewport(viewport(height=.8, width=.8))
print(gg, newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
```

Also like a histogram, a density plot encodes **data summaries**,
rather than raw data values,
to visual features (@tbl-density-stats).
In the case of a histogram, the data summary values are counts within bins
(@tbl-hist-stats) and each data summary produces a separate bar.
In the case of a density plot, the data summary produces density estimates
and these are encoded to a single data symbol, a line, to create
a **visual shape**.
The density estimates are encoded to the horizontal and vertical **positions**
of a single line data symbol.
The visual shape allows us to decode summaries of the density estimates.
For example, whether there is a single maximum density and how the density
changes to either side of that peak.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-density-stats
#| tbl-cap: A table of density estimates at a sample of values over the range of the number of points scored by Tier One nations in Rugby World Cup matches.  These data summaries are the values that are encoded to visual features to produce the density plot in @fig-density.  There are 512 rows of values, but only the first 6 are shown here.
d <- density(rwcAll$scored, from=min(rwcAll$scored), to=max(rwcAll$scored))
dStats <- cbind(scored=d$x, density=d$y)
kable(head(dStats), digits=c(2, 4))
```

@fig-data-stat-vis-shape-stat shows the path from raw data values to
data summaries (density estimates), which are encoded
as the visual features (horizontal
and vertical position) of a visual shape (a line)
in a density plot and
the summary information that we can decode from the visual shape.
We cannot decode the raw data values from a density plot, nor
can we very easily decode the data summaries (the density estimates).
The only real purpose of the data symbol in a density plot is to 
allow us to decode **summaries** of the data summaries, which are
visual features of the density estimates (like the number of peaks
and where the peaks occur).

::: {#fig-data-stat-vis-shape-stat}
::: {.content-visible when-format=pdf layout-ncol=2}
\includegraphics[scale=0.5]{Diagrams/data-stat-vis-shape-stat.png}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format=html layout-ncol=2}
![](Diagrams/data-stat-vis-shape-stat.png)
:::

A density plot encodes data summaries to visual features to create a visual
shape from which we can decode **summaries** of the data summaries.
:::

> A density plot is effective because it conveys high-level features of
  density estimates of the raw data.

Another commonality between density plots and histograms is that we get to
choose how the data summaries are calculated from the raw data values.
In the case of a density plot, we must choose a *kernel* and a *bandwidth*,
both of which affect the smoothness of the density estimates.
In other words, the choice of kernel and bandwidth
affects the shape of the line data symbol and that affects
the data summaries that we will decode (peaks, slopes, etc).
In a histogram, we may need to explore multiple choices of bin width
and in a density plot we may need to explore more than one kernel
and bandwidth (@sec-summary-caveats).

For example, @fig-density-bandwidth shows a density plot of the same data 
as @fig-density, but with a smaller bandwidth.  The resulting density
curve is much less smooth and so different data summaries can be decoded
from the visual shape.  This density curve looks a lot more like
the histogram with a narrow bin width in @fig-hist-thin;  we can decode
a possible second mode and we can even begin to 
decode peaks at individual numbers of points scored.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-density-bandwidth
#| fig-cap: A density plot of the points scored per game by Tier One nations at Rugby World Cups.  This is a variation of @fig-density using a much narrower bandwidth, so the density curve is much less smooth.
gg <- ggplot(rwcAll) +
    geom_density(aes(scored), colour="black", linewidth=1, adjust=.25) +
    scale_x_continuous(name="points scored") +
    theme(axis.title.y=element_blank(),
          axis.text.y=element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.y=element_blank())
pushViewport(viewport(height=.8, width=.8))
print(gg, newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
```

A final point about density plots, especially in comparison to histograms
is that it is more effective to present multiple density curves,
rather than multiple histograms.
This is demonstrated in @fig-multiple-density and @fig-multiple-hist.
Multiple histograms overlap each other, which makes it difficult
to perceive the separate histograms and this is not satisfactorily 
solved by adding semitransparency.
By comparison, multiple density curves create very little
overlap, and even though the orange curve passes "under" the blue curve,
we effortlessly perceive the orange curve as a single, coherent shape
(@sec-visual-model-groups).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-multiple-density
#| fig-cap: Density plots of the points scored per game by Tier One nations at Rugby World Cups, broken down by hemisphere.
gg <- ggplot(rwcAll) +
    geom_density(aes(scored, colour=hemisphere), linewidth=1) +
    scale_x_continuous(name="points scored") +
    scale_colour_discrete(guide=guide_legend(reverse=TRUE)) +
    theme(axis.title.y=element_blank(),
          axis.text.y=element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.y=element_blank())
pushViewport(viewport(height=.8, width=.8))
print(gg, newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-multiple-hist
#| fig-cap: Histograms of the points scored per game by Tier One nations at Rugby World Cups, broken down by hemisphere.
breaks <- seq(0, 105, by=5)
gg <- ggplot(rwcAll) +
    geom_histogram(aes(scored, colour=hemisphere, fill=hemisphere), 
                   breaks=breaks, alpha=.2, position="identity") +
    scale_colour_discrete(guide=guide_legend(reverse=TRUE)) +
    scale_fill_discrete(guide=guide_legend(reverse=TRUE)) +
    scale_x_continuous(name="points scored") +
    scale_y_continuous(expand=expansion(c(0, .05)))
pushViewport(viewport(height=.8, width=.8))
print(gg, newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
```

## Visual features of visual shapes {#sec-vis-shape-feature}

We have emphasised that a data symbol like a line in a line plot
is the result of encoding multiple data values as the **positions**
that the line is drawn between.  This results in a **visual shape** that
is more effective for decoding **data summaries** rather than decoding
the individual data values.

However, the examples that we have seen in @fig-line and 
@fig-multiple-density also involve another encoding: qualitative
data values, like ethnic group or hemisphere, are encoded as the
**colour** of the lines.
This encoding is consistent across the entire data symbol.
In effect, there is a simple encoding of qualitative data values
to a basic **visual feature** of the visual shape.

This means that it is possible to decode individual data values,
such as ethnic group or hemisphere, from a visual shape
if the data values have been encoded as a single consistent
visual feature of the visual shape (@fig-visual-feature-decode).

## Aspect ratio {#sec-aspect-ratio}

@fig-aspect shows a variation on @fig-line using a different 
**aspect ratio**---the height of the plot divided by the width of the plot.
@fig-line has an aspect ratio of 1 (the plot region is square), but 
@fig-aspect has an aspect ratio of only 0.2 (the plot region
is much shorter than it is wide).

@fig-aspect shows that the aspect ratio of the plot has a large
effect on the visual shapes of the data symbols, 
which means that the aspect ratio has
a large effect on the data summaries that we decode from the visual 
shapes.  For example, in @fig-aspect, we can still see a general downward
trend in three of the lines, with one line increasing.
However, the peak or jump in values at 2020 is much less obvious.
In other words, we decode different data summaries from @fig-aspect 
compared to @fig-line purely because of the difference in aspect ratio.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-aspect
#| fig-height: 1.5
#| fig-cap: A line plot of the number of offenders per year in different ethnic groups from 2011 to 2021.
gg <- ggplot(crimeGroup) +
    geom_line(aes(year, count, colour=group)) +
    scale_x_continuous(name=NULL, breaks=seq(2012, 2020, 2)) +    
    scale_y_continuous(expand=expansion(c(.2, .2))) +
    scale_colour_npg(name="ethnic group")
pushViewport(viewport(width=.8, height=.9))
print(gg, newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
```

There is no single rule for what the correct aspect ratio should be,[^banking]
so we may need to experiment with more than one aspect ratio 
to check what visual shapes are produced and whether 
it is possible to decode the features of interest.

[^banking]:
    The *median-absolute-slope criterion* suggests choosing 
    an aspect ratio such that the median absolute slope of the line segments
    between points is $45^{\circ}$
    (also known as the *45 degree banking rule*)
    [@Cleveland-banking].
    This is shown to produce the most accurate decoding of slopes.    

@fig-scatter-aspect demonstrates that a similar problem exists for
decoding data summaries from scatter plots (@sec-integral).
These plots encode the number of offloads (a fancy pass under
pressure in rugby) as the horizontal position of data points and
the number of tries (scoring actions) as the vertical position.
The correlation between the two measures can be decoded from the
emergent position in space of the data points.
The data is exactly the same for all four plots.

The decoding of trends in the points on a scatter plot has similarities
to the decoding of trends from visual shapes in a line plot[^virtual-lines]
and the shapes that we decode from a collection of data points are also
affected by the aspect ratio of a plot.
For example, the top-left plot in @fig-scatter-aspect suggests a stronger
relationship between offloads and tries than the bottom-left plot
simply because the trend appears flatter in the bottom-left plot
and that is solely thanks to the lower aspect ratio of the bottom-left plot.

[^virtual-lines]:
    @Cleveland-banking draws on the idea of *virtual lines* between the
    data points, from
    @marr1982vision and @stevens1978computation,
    to relate the decoding of trends from lines in a line plot with 
    the decoding of trends from data points in a scatter plot.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-scatter-aspect
#| fig-cap: A scatter plot of the number of times a team breaks through the opposition defence and the number of tries that a team scores (both are per-game averages) for teams at the 2023 Rugby World Cup.
gg1 <- ggplot(RWCperGame) +
    geom_point(aes(offloads, tries))
gg2 <- ggplot(RWCperGame) +
    geom_point(aes(offloads, tries)) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand=expansion(.4)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand=expansion(.4))
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(width=.8, layout=grid.layout(2, 2, heights=c(3, 1))))
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.col=1, layout.pos.row=1))
print(gg1,
      newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.col=2, layout.pos.row=1))
print(gg2,
      newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.col=1, layout.pos.row=2))
print(gg1, newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.col=2, layout.pos.row=2))
print(gg2,
      newpage=FALSE)
popViewport()
```

A related issue is the amount of empty space around the data points in
a scatter plot.  IN @fig-scatter-aspect, 
the relationship appears stronger in the top-right
plot compared to the top-left plot simply because the data points
are clustered more densely thanks to the different ranges on the plot 
axes.[^white-space]

[^white-space]: 
    @cleveland1994elements states that "our estimation of
    correlation is strongly affected by the area of the data rectangle relative
    to the area of the scale-line rectangle" and provides
    demonstrations (Figure 4.15 and 4.16).

## Decoding visual shapes {#sec-vis-shape-decode}

As we saw in @sec-vis-shape-feature, if data values are encoded
as a single, consistent visual feature of a visual shape, 
for example the colour of a line, then the original data values
can be decoded from the basic visual feature, as described in earlier
chapters for simpler data symbols like bars.

For data values that are encoded as different values of a visual
feature, such as the positions that a line is drawn between,
decoding from a visual shape results in
data summaries (@fig-data-vis-shape-decode),
for example peaks and valleys.
The visual system's ability to rapidly and effortlessly identify a wide range
of data summaries is part of why data visualisation is so effective.
It is difficult to calculate data summaries numerically from the raw data
with the same flexibility.[^anomaly-detection]
On the downside, as we saw in @sec-summary-decode and @sec-decode-combine,
the huge range of possible data summaries means that
less is known about how accurately we can decode
any particular data summary.

[^anomaly-detection]:
    The survey of anomaly-detection techniques by 
    @anomaly-detection gives a sense of how difficult it
    is to provide a general-purpose numerical technique
    for detecting features of interest in data values.

There is experimental support for the 
intuitive sense that we can perform well at 
decoding qualitative features from
shapes, such as peaks and valleys, as well as decoding ordinal 
comparisons, such as steeper and shallower.[^trends]
However, as @sec-aspect-ratio demonstrated, the decoding of slopes is
limited to *physical* slopes,
which are dependent on the aspect ratio, rather than 
decoding absolute rates of change in the data.[^slope-accuracy]

[^trends]:
    @proma2025visualstenographyfeaturerecreation showed that
    people are good at reproducing (therefore identifying) trends, 
    peaks, and valleys, if less so at reproducing 
    periodicity, noise/variability.
        
    @regression-by-eye showed that decoding of trends from line plots
    (and scatter plots) is quite accurate, at least
    relative to ordinary-least-squares models.

[^slope-accuracy]:    
    @Cleveland-banking points out that
    the accuracy of decoding slopes is only relevant to comparing the
    *relative steepness* of different regions of a line.  This is not
    accuracy in terms of decoding the actual rate of change in the
    data.  For that purpose, we should encode the actual rate of change
    directly.

## Case study: Box plots

@fig-box-shape shows box plots of the number of points scored by
Tier One nations at Rugby World Cup matches.
We have discussed box plots previously as examples of data visualisations
that encode data summaries to data symbols (@sec-box-plot).
For example, the median points scored is encoded as the horizontal position of
a thick vertical line for each team.
The only raw data values that are directly encoded are the outliers,
which are encoded as the horizontal position of data points for a few teams.
A box plot is effective for decoding the median for each team
because the median has been encoded as basic visual features of 
simple data symbol.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-box-shape
#| fig-cap: Box plots of the number of points scored by Tier One nations at Rugby World Cups.
rwcScored <- rwcAll
rwcScored$team <- reorder(rwcScored$team, rwcScored$scored, median)
ggplot(rwcScored) +
    geom_boxplot(aes(scored, team))
```

Box plots are also examples of encoding more than one data value 
(or data summary) to a single data symbol.
For each team, we have a complex data symbol made up of a rectangle and
horizontal and vertical lines, plus possibly some data points.
This creates a visual shape that allows us to decode additional
data summaries.  For example, some box plots, like the one for England, 
are symmetric, with the median
line at the center of the rectangle and with horizontal lines 
of similar lengths to either side.
Other box plots, like the one for Argentina, are asymmetric,
with the median towards one end of the rectangle and a longer horizontal
line to one side.
In other words, we can decode information about the skewness of the data
from the visual shape (@fig-data-vis-shape-decode).

## Dangers of visual shapes

@fig-zacks shows two data visualisations of average heights for males and 
females.  We have already discussed that it is easier to decode the
individual average height values from the bar plot because each average 
height is encoded as its own visual feature---the height of one bar.
We have also discussed that it is easier to decode trends from
a line plot (@sec-line-plots).

However, in @fig-zacks, the temptation to decode a trend from 
the line plot is in fact misleading. 
A line implies continuity, in this case even a linear trend.
However, the data values on the x-axis 
are qualitative categories (biological sex), rather than a continuum.
This means that decoding a trend from females to males
does not actually make sense.[^zacks]

[^zacks]:
    The data visualisations are based on Figure 2 from @Zacks1999.
    An example of one subject's decoding of the line plot was:
    "The more male a person is, the taller he/she is"    

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-zacks
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig.width: 4
#| fig-cap: Two data visualisations of average heights of females and males.
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - A bar plot supports decoding individual values.
#|   - A line plot supports decoding trends.
zacks <- data.frame(sex=c("Female", "Male"), height=c(45, 55))
gg <- ggplot(zacks, aes(sex, height)) +
    scale_y_continuous(name="Height (inches)", limits=c(0, 60),
                       expand=expansion(c(0, .1))) +
    scale_x_discrete(name=NULL)
gg1 <- gg +
    geom_col()
gg2 <- gg +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line(group=1)
gg1
gg2
```

A visual shape can be decoded to a data summary, but that is only
useful if the data summary is appropriate and not misleading 
(@fig-data-vis-shape-lie).

::: {#fig-data-vis-shape-lie}
::: {.content-visible when-format=pdf layout-ncol=2}
\includegraphics[scale=0.5]{Diagrams/data-vis-shape-lie.png}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format=html layout-ncol=2}
![](Diagrams/data-vis-shape-lie.png)
:::

Encoding data values to the visual features of a complex shape 
may not be effective if the complex shape decodes to unhelpful
or misleading information.
:::

@fig-gap shows another example of an undesirable shape decoding.
The two curves in @fig-gap are identical except that one has been
shifted vertically.  In other words, the vertical distance between
the two lines is constant.
In a data visualisation, we are typically interested in that
vertical distance:  what is the difference in *y* between
the two lines?

However, the natural decoding of the distance between the lines
focuses on the perpendicular distance, so the two lines appear
to be converging.[^gap-decode]  In other words, we decode the shape of the gap
between the lines to be a narrowing gap.

[^gap-decode]:
    This decoding of the difference between lines is described in
    @cleveland-science.  The recommended solution is to encode the
    difference between the lines, rather than requiring the viewer
    to perform the subtraction visually. 
    @gleicher-2011 call that solution *explicit encoding*.

    @validation-by-eye describe a similar issue with estimating 
    the line of best fit from data points in a scatter plot.
    Their results showed a bias towards orthogonal distance to the line 
    of best fit rather than vertical distance.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-gap
#| fig-cap: The two lines in this plot are just the same curve shifted vertically---the vertical distance between the lines in constant.  However, we decode the visual shape between the lines as a decrease in the gap between the lines.
df <- data.frame(x=1:100, y=(1:100)^3, y2=(1:100)^3+100000)
ggplot(df) +
    geom_line(aes(x, y)) +
    geom_line(aes(x, y2)) +
    theme(axis.title=element_blank(),
          axis.text=element_blank(),
          axis.ticks=element_blank(),
          aspect.ratio=1)
```

## Non-linear encodings {#sec-shape-non-linear}

@fig-arrivals shows time series plots of the number of 
international arrivals to New Zealand over the last century.[^peter-ellis]
@fig-arrivals-1 employs a linear scale on the y-axis and, because
the amount of international travel has changed so dramatically over time,
it is impossible to decode any detail from the first half of the 
twentieth century.

[^peter-ellis]:
    These plots are based on plots posted by Peter Ellis on a
    [StackExchange thread](https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/27951/when-are-log-scales-appropriate).
    The data are from [Stats NZ](https://infoshare.stats.govt.nz/)
    and licensed by Stats NZ for reuse under the 
    [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) licence.

We saw in @sec-non-linear-pos that one approach in this sort of situation
is to use a non-linear scale.
@fig-arrivals-2 uses this approach by employing a 
log (base 10) scale on the y-axis.
The advantage of the non-linear scale is clear:  it is now possible to
see details in the data for the first half of the twentieth century.
For example, we can now see the effect of the Second World War (1939--1945),
in addition to the effect of the COVID pandemic (2020--2021),
and we can see that the seasonal patterns are similar
over time.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-arrivals
#| layout-nrow: 2
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: Figures reproduced from @Zacks1999
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - linear y-axis scale
#|   - log (base 10) y-axis scale
arrivals <- read.csv("Data/ITM330701_20251022_043600_58.csv", skip=2,
                     header=FALSE, col.names=c("month", "count"))
arrivals$date <- as.Date(paste0(arrivals$month, "-01"),
                         format="%YM%m-%d")
ticks <- seq(0, 500000, 100000)
ggplot(arrivals) +
    geom_line(aes(date, count), linewidth=.5) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks=ticks, 
                       labels=format(ticks, scientific=FALSE, big.mark=","),
                       name=NULL,
                       sec.axis=dup_axis(labels=format(ticks, scientific=FALSE,
                                                       big.mark=",", 
                                                       trim=TRUE)))
ticks <- c(50, 100, 500, 1000, 5000, 10000, 
           50000, 100000, 500000)
ggplot(arrivals) +
    geom_line(aes(date, count), linewidth=.5) +
    scale_y_continuous(trans="log10",
                       breaks=ticks,
                       labels=format(ticks, scientific=FALSE, big.mark=","),
                       name=NULL,
                       sec.axis=dup_axis(labels=format(ticks, scientific=FALSE,
                                                       big.mark=",", 
                                                       trim=TRUE)))
```

An important point is that 
*all* of these decodings are from the visual shapes in @fig-arrivals-2.
We are able to decode an overall trend, local dips within the trend, and
regular spikes within the overall trend.

However, as we pointed out in @sec-non-linear-pos, the decoding of 
simple visual features is compromised by the use of a non-linear scale.
For example, it is very difficult to decode the final value of the 
time series in @fig-arrivals-2 because the same distance between
the tick marks on the y-axis does not represent the same difference in
data values (as emphasised by the choice of tick mark labels).
As we can see from @fig-arrivals-1, the final data value in the time
series is *not* half-way between 100,000 and 500,000.

It is *possible* to decode quantitative values from @fig-arrivals-2.
For example, the height of the seasonal changes remained fairly constant
over time.
However, that is an observation about the *logged* data, not the raw data 
values.[^log-ratio]
The danger of a log scale is that our natural decoding of position
and length is now incorrect.
For example, (in the absence of @fig-arrivals-1) we might be tempted to 
incorrectly decode 
from @fig-arrivals-2 that the absolute seasonal change in arrivals 
has remained constant over time.
In other words, the natural decoding of simple visual features can be
misleading in the presence of a non-linear scale.

[^log-ratio]:
    This observation does have a sensible interpretation: the consistent
    difference in logged values sugests that the size of seasonal changes is
    consistent *relative to* the absolute size of arrivals.  In other words the
    seasonal change in arrivals *divided by* the absolute number of arrivals is
    consistent over time.  However, that interpretation is not a simple,
    sub-conscious decoding of visual features; it requires a more sophisticated
    mental effort and a self-discipline to ignore the more naive
    decoding.


## Case study:  log-log plots

@fig-log-log-1 shows a scatter plot of metabolic rate versus body mass
for a wide range of lifeforms.[^kleibers-data]
Because of the very wide range of body mass values and metabolic rates,
with the largest animals being many orders of magnitude larger than
the smallest bacteria, almost all of the data is crushed into the
bottom-left corner.

[^kleibers-data]:
    These data are from @deCastro2025.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-log-log-1
#| fig-cap: Body mass versus metabolic rate for a wide variety of lifeforms. 
FieldMR <- read.csv("Data/FieldMR_SciDataPub.csv")
FieldMR <- subset(FieldMR, !(Kingdom %in% c("", "Unknown")) & !is.na(FMR_kJ_d))
kleiber <- read.table("Data/kleiber-mass-rate.txt", col.names=c("mass", "rate"))
template <- ggplot(FieldMR) +
    geom_point(aes(Mass_g, FMR_kJ_d, colour=Kingdom), alpha=.2) +
    scale_colour_discrete(guide=guide_legend(ncol=1, 
                                             override.aes=list(alpha=.8))) +
    grid_panel(textGrob("metabolic rate\n(kJ/day)", 
                        x=unit(-2, "mm"), 
                        y=1, just=c("right", "top"),
                        gp=gpar(fontfamily="mono", fontsize=10, lineheight=1)))+
    grid_panel(textGrob("mass (g)", 
                        x=1, just=c("left", "top"),
                        y=unit(-2, "mm"),
                        rot=-90,
                        gp=gpar(fontfamily="mono", fontsize=10))) +
    coord_cartesian(clip="off") +
    theme(aspect.ratio=1,
          text=element_text(family="mono"),
          axis.title=element_blank(),
          axis.text.x=element_text(angle=-90, hjust=0, vjust=.5, size=8),
          legend.title=element_blank(),
          legend.key.size=unit(4, "mm"),
          legend.position="right",
          legend.justification="top")
template + 
    scale_x_continuous(name="mass (g)") +
    scale_y_continuous(name="metabolic rate", breaks=seq(0, 40000, 10000)) +
    theme(plot.margin=margin(5, 0, 30, 0))
```

@fig-log-log-2 shows the same data, but this time with log (base 10) scales
on both axes.  While there is still considerable overlap, thanks
to the large number of observations, we can now see data for the
other Kingdoms beyond Animalia.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-log-log-2
#| fig-cap: Body mass versus metabolic rate for a wide variety of lifeforms.  Log (base 10) scales.
ticksy <- 10^(seq(-7, 1, 4))
formatTicks <- function(ticks) {
    labels <- format(ticks, scientific=FALSE, big.mark=",")
    startZero <- grepl(" 0[.]", labels)
    labels <- ifelse(startZero, 
                      gsub(" 0[.]", " .", labels),
                      labels)
    endZeros <- gregexpr("0+$", labels)
    endZero <- sapply(endZeros, function(x) x != -1)
    endSpace <- ifelse(endZero,
                       sapply(endZeros, 
                              function(x) {
                                  if (x == -1) {
                                      ""
                                  } else {
                                      paste(rep(" ", attr(x, "match.length")),
                                            collapse="")
                                  }
                              }),
                       "")
    labels <- ifelse(endZero,
                      paste0(gsub("0+$", "", labels), endSpace),
                      labels)
    gsub("[.] ", "  ", labels)
}
labelsy <- formatTicks(ticksy)
labelsx <- formatTicks(ticksy)
template + 
    scale_x_continuous(name="mass", transform="log10",
                       breaks=ticksy,
                       labels=labelsx) +
    scale_y_continuous(name="metabolic rate", transform="log10",
                       breaks=ticksy,
                       labels=labelsy)
    ## kg vs g and kcal vs kJ
    ## geom_point(aes(mass*1000, rate*4.2), data=kleiber, alpha=.5)
```

What we can also see in @fig-log-log-2
is a clear **visual shape** amongst the data symbols---a
strong linear relationship.
It is useful to be able to decode this linear shape
from a plot with log scales because it indicates a
power relationship between the two variables, in this case
metabolic rate and body mass.[^kleibers-law]
It is also possible to decode ordinal information, such as the fact that
animals are larger and use more energy than bacteria.

[^kleibers-law]:
    This power relationship between metabolic rate and body mass
    is known as *Kleiber's Law* [@kleiber].

However, decoding the basic **position** of data symbols from a plot
with log scales is very difficult because equal steps
along either axis do *not* decode to equal steps between data values
(as indicated by the axis labels).  
For example, we cannot easily decode *how much* bigger animals are than 
bacteria.
There is even danger, for the
uninitiated, in decoding the linear **visual shape** because it does *not*
decode to a linear relationship between the raw data values.

Once again, we have a data visualisation that can be usefully decoded in a 
particular way, but which also contains encodings that are difficult
and potentially misleading.
